about.title: Marina Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Falls happen fast, but the aftermath can drag on for months, especially if the property owner disputes what caused your injury. Whether you slipped on a wet floor near Del Monte Boulevard, tripped on uneven pavement off Imjin Parkway, or fell due to poor lighting in a stairwell, California law asks a specific question: did the property owner know, or should they have known, about the hazard, and did they fail to fix it or warn you? That's the heart of a premises liability case here in Marina. Because evidence like surveillance footage, incident reports, and even the condition of a walkway can change or disappear quickly, timing matters. LawProactive doesn't handle claims directly, but we connect injured residents with an independent attorney who can evaluate what happened, gather evidence while it's still available, and explain your options without any upfront cost or obligation to move forward.

whyChoose.title: Why Marina Residents Turn to LawProactive

items.title: Notice Is Everything
items.desc: California premises cases hinge on proving the owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard. An attorney can help identify prior complaints, maintenance logs, or repeat incidents that establish that notice.

items.title: Video and Evidence Fade Fast
items.desc: Many Marina retailers and apartment complexes overwrite surveillance footage within days or weeks. Acting quickly can mean the difference between having proof of the hazard and having none.

items.title: Your Share of Fault Doesn't End Your Claim
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, you can still recover damages even if you were partly responsible for the fall, though your share of fault will reduce the amount recovered.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Marina?
items.answer: In most cases, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a public entity, such as a city building or school, the deadline is much shorter and requires an early claim. Because these timelines are strict, it's worth having an attorney review your situation sooner rather than later.

items.question: What if I fell at a store off Reservation Road or Imjin Parkway but I'm not sure who owns the property?
items.answer: That's common, and it's something an attorney can sort out through public records and lease agreements. Commercial corridors often involve a property owner separate from the business tenant, and liability can depend on who was responsible for maintenance. An independent attorney can identify the right parties before any deadlines pass.

items.question: Do I need photos or a report from the store to have a valid claim?
items.answer: Photos, witness names, and an incident report all strengthen a claim, but their absence doesn't automatically end one. Surveillance footage, maintenance records, or prior complaints can sometimes fill in the gaps. The sooner you speak with an attorney, the better the chance of preserving whatever evidence still exists.
